adjudication_records.issue_text: #1 | app/controllers/groups_controller.rb:28 | The unchanged members endpoint changes its response from a top-level user array to `{members, meta}` without versioning; existing API and plugin consumers can fail immediately | api-contract | 100

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows the members endpoint in groups_controller.rb changing from `render_serialized(members.to_a, GroupUserSerializer)` which returns a flat array of users, to `render json: { members: serialize_data(...), meta: { total, limit, offset } }` which returns an object with 'members' and 'meta' keys. This is a breaking change to the API response format - any existing consumers expecting an array will now receive an object and will fail. This is a real API contract breaking change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #2 | app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:37 | `update` no longer honors nested PUT `group[...]` or PATCH `changes[...]` payloads and can silently set omitted `visible` to false; existing automation may ignore requested changes and hide groups | api-contract | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the old `update` method had `update_put` which accessed params via `params[:group][:alias_level]`, `params[:group][:visible]`, etc. The new `update` method accesses params directly: `params[:alias_level]`, `params[:visible]`, etc. This is indeed a breaking API change - any existing clients sending nested parameters like `group[visible]=true` will have those parameters ignored. Additionally, `group.visible = params[:visible] == "true"` will set visible to false if the parameter is not provided (since nil == "true" is false). This is a real API contract change that could break existing integrations and silently hide groups.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #3 | app/controllers/groups_controller.rb:22 | The public members view performs only one 50-member fetch and exposes no pagination controls; members after the first 50 become unreachable | correctness | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the groups_controller.rb members action now accepts limit and offset parameters and returns pagination metadata (total, limit, offset). The group.js model has been updated with findMembers() that accepts limit/offset and stores pagination state. However, examining the public group members template (discourse/templates/group/members.hbs), it only shows a table iterating over 'members' with no pagination controls visible. The admin-group.js controller has next/previous actions and pagination UI, but the public group-members route (discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6) just calls model.findMembers() once without any pagination actions. The public members view lacks pagination controls, so users beyond the first 50 would indeed be unreachable in the public view.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #4 | app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:38 | The legacy PATCH route remains active but ignores membership changes and sets omitted `visible` to false while returning success | correctness | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the old code had separate `update_patch` and `update_put` methods with a check `if request.patch?` to route between them. The new `update` method completely replaces this logic and only handles PUT-style updates (setting alias_level, visible, name). The diff shows the old `update_patch` method being removed, which handled incremental add/delete of members. However, the routes.rb changes show new dedicated endpoints for member management: `delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member'` and `put 'members' => 'groups#add_members'`. The finding claims the PATCH route 'remains active' but the diff doesn't show the routes configuration for the main groups resource - we only see the new member routes being added. The new `update` method at line 38 handles both PATCH and PUT requests the same way now, which is intentional since membership is handled separately. The `visible` parameter defaults to false when not provided (`params[:visible] == 'true'`), but this is consistent with the old code. This appears to be an intentional refactoring where membership management was moved to separate endpoints, not a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #5 | app/assets/javascripts/discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6:11 | The public route fetches only the model’s default 50 members without pagination controls, silently publishing an incomplete roster for larger groups | adversarial | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for group-members.js.es6, the route calls model.findMembers() which sets up pagination properties (limit, offset, user_count) on the model. However, examining the template group/members.hbs, it only iterates over 'members' without any pagination controls visible in the template. The admin group template has pagination controls (previous/next buttons with currentPage/totalPages), but the public group/members.hbs template does not have these controls. This means for the public group members view, users can only see the first 50 members with no way to navigate to see more. This is a real functionality gap - the backend supports pagination but the public UI doesn't expose it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #6 | app/controllers/groups_controller.rb:22 | The client-controlled page limit has no server-side maximum, allowing large groups to be fully loaded and serialized in one request | performance | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff in app/controllers/groups_controller.rb lines 21-35, the code shows `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` with no maximum cap. A client can pass an arbitrarily large limit value (e.g., limit=1000000), which would cause the server to load and serialize a potentially huge number of user records in a single request. This is a real performance/DoS vulnerability - there's no server-side validation to cap the limit parameter to a reasonable maximum value.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #7 | app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:71 | Bulk add accepts an unbounded username list and performs serial user lookups and membership writes, creating linear database load and timeout risk | performance | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the add_members method in the diff (lines 63-77 of groups_controller.rb), it accepts a 'usernames' parameter, splits it by comma, and iterates through each username performing a User.find_by_username lookup and group.add operation. There is no limit on the number of usernames that can be passed. This is a real performance concern - an attacker or user could pass thousands of usernames, causing linear database queries and writes. However, this is an admin-only controller (inherits from Admin::AdminController), which significantly reduces the risk since only admins can access it. The finding is technically accurate about the unbounded nature, but the severity is mitigated by admin-only access. It's still a real issue as even admin endpoints should have reasonable limits to prevent accidental or intentional DoS.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #8 | app/controllers/groups_controller.rb:22 | The endpoint now defaults to 50 members instead of all custom-group members or 200 automatic-group members; callers without pagination silently receive incomplete results | api-contract | 100

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the members endpoint changed from returning up to 200 members for automatic groups (or all members for custom groups) to always returning a default of 50 members with pagination. This is a real API contract change - existing callers that expected to receive all members (or up to 200) will now only receive 50 by default. The old code had `limit = (params[:limit] || 200).to_i` for automatic groups and returned all members for non-automatic groups. The new code uses `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` for all groups. This is a breaking change for API consumers who don't implement pagination.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #9 | app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:24 | `create` stops accepting nested `group[name, visible, usernames]` parameters without compatibility handling; existing clients can submit blank names and lose create-with-members behavior | api-contract | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the create method changes from expecting nested parameters like `params[:group][:name]` and `params[:group][:usernames]` to flat parameters like `params[:name]` and `params[:visible]`. The old code was `group.name = (params[:group][:name] || '').strip` and `group.usernames = params[:group][:usernames]`, while the new code is `group.name = (params[:name] || '').strip` and `group.visible = params[:visible] == 'true'`. Additionally, the `usernames` parameter handling is completely removed from create - the new create method doesn't handle usernames at all. This is a real API contract change that would break existing clients sending nested parameters. However, looking at the JavaScript changes, the client code is also updated to use the new API format (`group.create()` now uses `this.asJSON()` which returns flat parameters). The finding correctly identifies that the API contract changed and existing clients using the old format would fail. This is a real breaking change in the API.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #10 | app/assets/javascripts/admin/controllers/admin-group.js.es6:56 | The remove-member callback and add-members action discard mutation promises and attach no rejection handler; API failures become silent or unhandled | reliability | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the `removeMember` action at line 56 uses `bootbox.confirm` which is a UI confirmation dialog - it doesn't return a promise that needs handling. Inside the callback, `self.get('model').removeMember(member)` is called but its return value is not used. Similarly, `addMembers` at line 64 calls `this.get('model').addMembers(this.get('usernames'))` without handling the returned promise. Looking at the model's `removeMember` and `addMembers` methods, they return promises from AJAX calls. If these fail, there's no error handling - the promises are indeed discarded. However, the `removeMember` action returns the result of `bootbox.confirm()`, not the promise from the actual removal. The finding is partially correct - the promises from API calls are not being handled for errors, which could lead to silent failures. This is a real reliability issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #13 | app/assets/javascripts/discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6:11 | Public member loading moved from an awaited route hook to a fire-and-forget call, so rejected requests leave the page silently empty or stale | reliability | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for group-members.js.es6, the code changes from using afterModel (which returns a promise that the router waits for) to calling model.findMembers() in setupController without awaiting it. The old code: 'afterModel: function(model) { return model.findMembers().then(...) }' ensured the route waited for members to load. The new code: 'setupController: function(controller, model) { ... model.findMembers(); }' is fire-and-forget - if findMembers() fails, there's no error handling and the page would show empty/stale data. This is a real reliability issue where AJAX failures are silently ignored.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #14 | app/assets/javascripts/admin/controllers/admin-group.js.es6:37 | Pagination requests are not serialized or canceled while offset changes eagerly; out-of-order responses can render the wrong page | reliability | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the `next` and `previous` actions in admin-group.js.es6 set the offset on the group model and then call `group.findMembers()`. The `findMembers()` method in group.js makes an AJAX request and updates `members` when the response arrives. If a user clicks next/previous rapidly, multiple requests can be in flight simultaneously, and responses may arrive out of order. The last response to arrive will set the `members` property, which may not correspond to the current `offset` value. This is a real race condition - there's no request cancellation, no serialization of requests, and no check that the response matches the current offset before updating the UI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #15 | app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:71 | Multi-user addition is not transactional and has no partial-failure contract; a mid-operation failure can leave only part of the batch committed | reliability | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the add_members method in app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb lines 63-78, the code iterates through usernames and calls group.add(user) for each one, then calls group.save at the end. The finding claims this is not transactional and partial failures could leave only part of the batch committed. However, examining the code: group.add(user) likely adds users to the group's association, and group.save is called once at the end. If group.save fails, the changes wouldn't be persisted. The real issue is that group.add() might persist immediately depending on implementation (if it's a has_many through relationship with immediate persistence), but this is speculation about code not shown in the diff. The code shown does have a single save call at the end, which suggests it's trying to be atomic. Without seeing the Group#add implementation, we can't definitively say this is non-transactional. The finding is speculative about behavior not clearly demonstrated in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #17 | app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js:23 | `findMembers` clamps against stale client-side counts and does not correct the returned offset against the new total; removing the last member on a page can strand the UI out of range | correctness | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the findMembers function in group.js, the offset is clamped using: `var offset = Math.min(this.get("user_count"), Math.max(this.get("offset"), 0));`. This uses the client-side user_count before the AJAX call. After the call, the response updates user_count, limit, and offset from the server's meta data. The issue is that if a member is removed and user_count decreases, the client's stale user_count could allow an offset that's now out of range. However, the server returns the actual offset used in result.meta.offset, which gets set on the model. The real issue is the pre-request clamping uses potentially stale data, but the server response corrects this. The finding claims the UI can get 'stranded out of range' but the server-side pagination would handle this by returning valid data. The client-side clamping is just a pre-request optimization that may be slightly off, but the server response corrects the state. This is a minor edge case issue but not a significant correctness problem since the server response updates the offset.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #18 | app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js:30 | Concurrent member requests overwrite shared pagination state without a stale-response guard, allowing older responses to replace the current page | correctness | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the findMembers function in group.js, it makes an AJAX request and then calls setProperties to update user_count, limit, offset, and members. The concern is that if multiple requests are made (e.g., rapid clicking of next/previous), responses could arrive out of order and an older response could overwrite newer data. However, examining the code: (1) The next/previous actions check showingFirst/showingLast before proceeding, (2) The offset is set on the model before findMembers is called, and (3) The response updates the model with the server's actual offset value. While there's no explicit request cancellation or stale-response guard, this is a relatively minor race condition that would only occur with very rapid clicking. The code does update offset from the response (result.meta.offset), which provides some protection. This is a valid but minor concern - it's a real potential issue but the severity is low as it would self-correct on the next navigation action.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #19 | spec/controllers/admin/groups_controller_spec.rb:36 | The create test never submits or asserts `alias_level`, allowing `create` to drop the client-supplied alias policy while tests remain green | testing | 100

adjudication_records.issue_text: #20 | spec/controllers/admin/groups_controller_spec.rb:49 | Update coverage exercises only an automatic group and never validates the new flat payload for a normal group; the primary admin save contract can break undetected | testing | 100

The test doesn't verify that a normal (non-automatic) group can be updated with the new flat payload structure. adjudication_records.issue_text: #25 | app/controllers/groups_controller.rb:22 | The caller-controlled limit has no positive upper bound, creating a repeatable resource-exhaustion path against large visible groups | adversarial | 100

An attacker could pass an extremely large limit value (e.g., limit=1000000) to force the server to load and serialize a massive number of user records in a single request. adjudication_records.issue_text: #26 | app/assets/javascripts/admin/controllers/admin-group.js.es6:13 | Exact multiples of the page size create a nonexistent extra page and advance offset to `user_count`, rendering an empty final page | adversarial | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the totalPages calculation on line 13: `Math.floor(this.get("user_count") / this.get("limit")) + 1`. If user_count is exactly divisible by limit (e.g., 50 users with limit 50), this returns floor(50/50)+1 = 2 pages, but there's actually only 1 page of content. Similarly, currentPage calculation uses offset/limit+1. When on the last page with offset=0 for 50 users, currentPage=1 and totalPages=2, so showingLast would be false, allowing 'next' to advance offset to 50, which would show an empty page. This is a real off-by-one pagination bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #27 | app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js:30 | Member responses overwrite shared state regardless of request order; rapid navigation or mutation reloads can replace current data with stale results | adversarial | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the findMembers function in group.js, when the AJAX call completes it calls self.setProperties() to update members, user_count, limit, and offset on the model. The concern is that if multiple findMembers() calls are made in rapid succession (e.g., clicking next/previous quickly), the responses could arrive out of order and overwrite the current state with stale data. This is a real race condition - the code doesn't track which request corresponds to which offset, so a slow response from an earlier request could overwrite data from a later request. The setupController calls findMembers() without awaiting it, and the next/previous actions also call findMembers(). There's no cancellation of pending requests or sequence tracking to ensure only the latest response is applied.

adjudication_records.issue_text: #29 | app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js:47 | Membership mutation methods resolve before their refresh completes, leaving stale state without a handleable failure | correctness | 100

The methods return the outer AJAX promise which resolves when the add/remove operation completes, not when the member list refresh completes. However, this is not necessarily a bug - the caller gets notified when the mutation is done, and the UI will update when findMembers completes asynchronously. The finding claims this leaves 'stale state without a handleable failure', but the state will be updated when findMembers completes. The real issue would be if callers needed to know when the refresh was done, but looking at the usage in the controller actions (removeMember, addMembers), they don't chain on the returned promise for UI updates. This is more of a design consideration than a correctness bug.
